text: IMRAD assumes one authorial voice: everything in the text is attributed to the named authors, and methods are described in prose rather than executed.
A statement such as 'we used ChatGPT' does not tell a reader whether the model corrected commas or built the central thesis (ghost-thinking).
LEM replaces the single-voice IMRAD article with three separable layers: Human, Process and Reader.
The Claim Drift Index is the share of atomic claims in a rendering that are unsupported by, or contradict, the H layer.
Analytic steps are validated by re-execution; cognitive steps are validated by traceability of what the model proposed and what the author accepted, rejected or rewrote.
Two-tier logging records substantive cognitive steps in full with an override log and surface edits only as meta-tags.
A surface edit whose semantic delta exceeds a threshold, such as turning 'may suggest' into 'demonstrates', is escalated to substantive automatically.
LEM is adopted in three conformance levels: LEM-0 Analytic Provenance, LEM-1 Cognitive Provenance and LEM-2 Attested Provenance.
LEM-2 adds assurance, not scope: records are captured automatically and sealed in a hash chain so they cannot be curated after the fact.
Comparing LEM-1 declarations with LEM-2 captured records shows how far self-declared AI contribution departs from captured contribution.
LEM makes it measurable whether social scientists use AI as an idea generator or only as a grammar assistant.
The override log is the evidence that a human, not the model, decided what the paper claims.
The reference manuscript in the repository is this proposal documented in its own format at LEM-1.
